name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, I'm 27, and I'm a marketing assistant at Hearthpaw, a pet food brand that does dry food and treats for dogs and cats. I live with my boyfriend Pavel, who's an electrician, in a rented house on the edge of town. I've been at Hearthpaw almost two years, and last spring we were bought by a bigger food group, which everyone's still nervous about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my day is product copy: the descriptions on our website, the listings for the big online pet shops, the feeding guides on the back of the bag. I like it when I get the tone right, warm but not silly, because pet owners can smell nonsense. I've never used any of the AI writing tools; I tried once and didn't trust what it wrote about salmon content. What wears me out is the spreadsheets of ingredients and the fact that I'm slower than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, it was overhyped. At work I'd probably just nod and keep going, I don't make speeches. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because the routine stuff it does automate is my stuff. Listings and feeding guides are the most routine writing at Hearthpaw, the pet food brand I work for, and that routine writing is my stuff. And the new owners are already looking at merging our team with their other pet brand, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job carefully and try to be quicker, maybe by using templates I make myself. I'd add 50 a month to our savings, which are about two and a half months right now. And I'd keep an eye on the merger news without doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, if I'm honest. Nothing's changing in the world, but my own corner was already shaky before any of this. I'd feel like I was waiting for an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the new owners might merge teams. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two marketing teams, one set of jobs. They'd keep the senior people and probably one assistant, and I'm not the quickest assistant. The other team already uses AI for listings, I heard, which doesn't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Pavel say when you talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel says electricians are always needed and I could always do something else. He means it kindly. But I like my job, and I don't want to start again at 27.

say: I'd say the AI talk was **overhyped**, and leave it there.
I'd keep my head down at work and **post nothing**.
think: The **routine writing** AI does take is exactly her listings and guides.
The new owners may **merge teams**, AI or no AI.
do: Build her own **templates** to speed up listings.
Add **50 a month** to about two and a half months of savings.
feel: **Tense**, like she's waiting for an email.
Her corner was **already shaky** before AI came up.
S0.quote: Listings and feeding guides are the most routine writing at Hearthpaw, the pet food brand I work for, and that routine writing is my stuff.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from a **takeover**, not from AI.
She's **quiet** and won't speak up publicly.
Pavel's **trade job** gives her a safety net she doesn't want to lean on.

steps.text: Build her own templates for pet shop listings to work faster
Add 50 a month to the shared savings account
Watch the merger news before deciding anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business works, companies use whatever's cheaper. I wouldn't be angry online, but I'd tell friends I'm worried. At work I'd ask my manager, Helen, directly whether my role is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone within two years. Product listings and feeding guides are the first thing a tool can do, and the merged company will want one person checking it, not three writing it. And I'm the one who doesn't use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for work that's less about writing straight away, maybe customer events or working in a pet shop chain's head office. I'd cut our takeaways and the gym, which is about 120 a month. And I'd probably finally try the AI tools, because refusing them would make me look worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like the job I just got good at is being taken away right as I learned it. And it makes me feel old at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally try the tools. Why now, after not trusting them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because not using the AI tools would be the reason they let me go, not the tools themselves. I still don't trust what they write about ingredients. I'd use them and check every line, which is what I'd be paid for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose the job, how would the household manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel earns more than me, so we'd keep the house. But my two and a half months of savings would go on my share of the bills by spring. After that I'd be asking Pavel to carry me, and I really don't want that.

say: I'd say companies **use what's cheaper**; that's business.
I'd ask my manager directly if my **role is safe**.
think: Her job is **gone within two years**, she thinks.
As the one who **doesn't use tools**, she'd be cut first.
do: Look for **less writing-based** roles like events or pet chain head office.
Cut takeaways and the gym, saving about **120 a month**.
Finally try the **AI tools**, checking every line.
feel: **Heavy**, losing a job right as she got good at it.
S1.quote: Not using the AI tools would be the reason they let me go, not the tools themselves.
fieldNote: She shifts from refusing tools to **using them defensively**.
She's **pragmatic** and blames nobody, calling it business.
Leaning on **Pavel's income** is her deepest discomfort.

steps.text: Apply for events or head-office jobs at pet shop chains
Cancel takeaways and the gym to save 120 a month
Start using AI for listings and check every ingredient line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need some kind of plan from the government, quickly. I wouldn't march, but I'd vote for whoever has a sensible plan. At work I'd just say I'm worried, like everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job ends in 2028 and there's nothing I can do about it in two years. It's all screen work. The only bit that's hands-on is helping at the dog shows twice a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Pavel about whether I could be his apprentice or help in his business, doing the booking at first and then real wiring. That's hands-on, so it gets three more years. I'd stop all spending except basics, and I'd ask my parents if we could move in with them if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I don't change quickly, and this is the fastest change you can picture. I'd be lying if I said I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Becoming Pavel's apprentice. Would you actually want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm scared of ladders, but I'd rather learn to wire a socket than sit at home. And at least I'd be with Pavel, which would make it feel less like a defeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the booking side first. Doesn't AI take that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, the booking goes on day one. So it would have to be the hands-on side, straight away. That's even scarier.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan** quickly.
I'd **vote** for whoever has a sensible plan, not march.
think: Her job **ends in 2028**, with nothing she can do in two years.
Only the **dog shows**, twice a year, are hands-on.
do: Ask to become **Pavel's apprentice** doing real wiring.
Ask her parents about **moving in** if it gets bad.
feel: Scared of ladders but would **rather wire sockets** than sit home.
S2.quote: I'm scared of ladders, but I'd rather learn to wire a socket than sit at home.
fieldNote: She first reaches for **booking work**, then sees AI takes that too.
Her fallback is **Pavel's trade**, for the three-year robot gap.
**Parents** are the last safety net she'd ask for.

steps.text: Start learning wiring work as Pavel's apprentice
Cut household spending to rent, food and bills
Ask her parents if they could move in if money runs out
Vote for the party with a clear jobs plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so everyone should start now. I'd talk about it at work and maybe sign up for whatever training the company offers. Online I still wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd waste the first two years hoping it wasn't true. That's how I am. Then I'd panic in year three, which is exactly what I shouldn't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm being sensible, I'd look into training as a veterinary nurse in the first year, since I love animals and it's hands-on. I'd keep the Hearthpaw job while I study part-time. And I'd put every spare bit of money toward savings, aiming for five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frightened than the two-year one. There's a path if I'm brave enough to take it. I'm just not sure I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why veterinary nursing, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've spent two years writing about what dogs eat and I've realised I like the dogs more than the writing. It's hands-on, so it's got until 2034. And the vet down our road is always hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you starting in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and nerves. The course is part-time over three years, and I'd be the oldest in the class. Pavel would push me, though, he's good at that.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** to start now.
I'd sign up for any **company training** offered.
think: She'd **waste two years** hoping it wasn't true.
Then she'd **panic in year three**, which she knows is wrong.
do: Look into **veterinary nursing** training in the first year.
Study part-time while keeping the **Hearthpaw job**.
feel: **Worried**, but less frightened than the fast version.
Unsure she's **brave enough** to take the path.
S3.quote: I've spent two years writing about what dogs eat and I've realised I like the dogs more than the writing.
fieldNote: She predicts her **own delay** with striking honesty.
**Vet nursing** links her job to a hands-on future.
Pavel is the one who would **push her** to start.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time veterinary nursing course in the first year
Keep the Hearthpaw job while studying
Save toward five months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and people shouldn't panic. At work I'd say let's get trained up properly. I'd probably say it to my mum too, she worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have maybe five or six years left in marketing before it got thin. Ten years is long enough even for someone slow like me, but I'd still lose the job I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hearthpaw for a few years and save, then start the vet nursing course around year three or four. I'd also learn the AI tools, because I'd need to stay employed while I studied. Pavel and I would probably put off buying a house until I'd finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad but steady. I can see myself doing it, slowly. It's not the life I planned, but it's not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off the house. How long have you been saving for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year, but we've only got a small pot. Pavel wants to buy next year. I'd ask him to wait until I'm qualified, and he'd grumble but agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually start the course, or keep putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, honestly, I'd probably put it off for a bit. But Pavel would keep asking, and the dog would need feeding either way. I'd get there.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning**, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd tell colleagues we should all **get trained** properly.
think: She has maybe **five or six years** left in marketing.
She'd still **lose the job** she trained for.
do: Start **vet nursing** training around year three or four.
Learn the **AI tools** to stay employed while studying.
Put off **buying a house** until she's qualified.
feel: **Sad but steady**, seeing herself doing it slowly.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough even for someone slow like me, but I'd still lose the job I trained for.
fieldNote: The decade lets a **resistant** person change at her own pace.
She admits she'd **put off** the course for a while.
The **house purchase** becomes the main trade-off with Pavel.

steps.text: Start a vet nursing course around year three or four
Learn the AI listing tools to stay employed while studying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and two years is nothing. What would help is a proper course with some money while you do it, so I could train as a vet nurse without leaning on Pavel completely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that the takeover scares me as much as AI does. People talk about robots, but for me a new owner with a spreadsheet is the more real threat.

headlineQuote: People talk about robots, but for me a new owner with a spreadsheet is the more real threat.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old assistant** writing listings at a pet food brand, living with Pavel, an electrician.
She has **never used AI**, distrusting what it writes about ingredients.
A **takeover** by a bigger group already makes her job feel shaky.
In faster change she'd use the tools **defensively**, then look to hands-on work.
With time she'd retrain as a **veterinary nurse**, though she expects to delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she changes slowly and two years is nothing.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** so she could train as a vet nurse without leaning on Pavel completely.
